"An Act to Allow Certain Persons with a Permit to Carry Concealed
Handguns to Possess or Discharge a Firearm on School Property" Sponsored by Representative White
Greetings to the committee.
I am here today in full support of a unanimous "Ought to Pass" for LD885.
lt's high time we changed the Maine law that makes it illegal for adults to protect our children on school grounds. "Gun Free Zones" is one of the most
counterproductive type of laws ever passed. Simply posting signs and wishing for the best does not work.
lt's time to face the reality that sociopaths and lunatics with evil in their
hearts and minds will never, ever follow the rules or laws of others. Once they have set a goal of inflicting harm or death on innocent people, the only thing that will immediately stop them is to meet them with equal or greater force.
To think that a sign on a door or window will stop them is at best delusional, at worst, continuing to support them is being complicit in the death and
mayhem they invite. History has proven, time after time, after time, that
unprotected GFZs do not provide any safety whatsoever.
Approximately thirty years ago this body made the promise to protect our
children and up to today, it has remained just that, a promise. To merely
declare a particular place or area as being "Gun Free" without taking
measures to either enforce that or provide adequate protection to those people in that place or area does not fulfill that promise.
In the decades since, there has been much discussion about how to keep
that promise which has resulted in very little actual, effective action. The most dominant discussions have been to ban certain types of guns or to attempt to
restrict who can have guns.
As to banning so called "Assault Rifles", even if it happened it would not have
any measurable effect on the murder rate in the US or safety of our children.
As per the FBI, they are used in less than 300 murders annually of the over 14,000 committed. That is less than one percent and is also an argument by itself for another day. Also, there are approx. 30,000,000 of them already in

circulation and it would be a few more decades before they were all collected, even if that were possible. Guns are not going to just disappear or become illegal to possess anytime soon, probably not even in our lifetimes.
Regarding restrictions on who can possess firearms, that is a discussion that has been going on for decades and unless we can come up with a way to
foresee the future of each individual human, will continue to go on for decades more.
Hardening our schools would take billions of dollars that right now aren't
there and would take, again, decades to implement.
Hiring and training enough Law Enforcement to have them present in every school building in the state would also take years and massive amounts of money to get in place.
In the meantime, our children are still not adequately protected, and, in my
opinion, those other discussions are distracting our minds and resources from doing anything meaningful to that end.
Federal law has always had an exception from the GFSZA for permit holders
to carry on school grounds. Around 16 other states have always allowed it,
and 38 states have some form of it for proactive protection.
This is the most economical way to protect our children, it costs the taxpayer absolutely nothing! It is also the simplest and fastest way to finally give our children and school staff the means they need to protect themselves.
There are over 800 school campuses in Maine and all of them currently have
a sign on the door that basically says, "Please don't hurt me". Let's change
those signs to say, "Staff may be Armed". That type of sign, all by itself, is a greater deterrent than any GFZ sign has ever been. Truthfully, even if not one person on campus is armed it still does more to deter a would-be shooter
than the previous sign!
Most perpetrators of such heinous crimes are, more often than not,
cowards. There are many published accounts of them searching out the most vulnerable, unprotected targets they can find. Let's take that advantage away
from them!

There have been many reports of teachers putting themselves between the
shooter and the children. While that is a noble, valiant gesture, it does not protect the students. The reality is that they're merely sacrificing themselves first. If the adult in the room is willing to do that, let's at least give them back the choice of actually being able to protect themselves and our children.
There are always going to be "what ifs", but history and many studies say that
people with carry permits are overwhelmingly the politest, most law-abiding demographic in the US. Those studies were published by the Universities of Chicago and Harvard Law, the FBI and the CDC.
The rules of engagement for CCW holders are much higher than that of LEOs
or security personnel which, I believe, also plays a major role in why they almost always have little or no collateral casualties when they do engage an
active shooter. We also tend to train much, much more often with our carry
firearms than the majority of LEOs.
I have heard the words "common-sense" many times when referencing gun laws. LD885 is actually one most common-sense laws proposed of late when talking about gun laws. Having the adults present prepared with the means to
defend themselves should an incident occur would be one of the most
com mon-sense, cost effective things we can do to immediately provide
protection for our schools and children.
Again, I support an Ought to Pass vote for LD885.
Respectfully,
Bruce M Ashmore
Sgt USA, Ret.
Bucksport, ME

Dear Members of the Education Committee, I am a retired Maine school teacher with over 28 years of experience and I am a
mother and grandmother. We absolutely should not allow guns in our schools even in the hands of concealed weapons permit holders. There are many reasons why this is a bad idea which I would like to point out.
1) Getting a concealed weapons permit is not that difficult. Although some individuals may go to the shooting range to practice this does not qualify them to know what to do in a real active shooter situation. My husband is in law enforcement. Not only does he wear a bullet proof vest, he has hours of scenario training. These individuals have no training in assessing the danger or in implementing a plan of action and they, in their unexperienced state, would be around children, with a loaded weapon. In an active shooter situation how are law enforcement supposed to differentiate between them and the active shooter?
2) We don't know the mental state or stress that any of these individuals may be under. Just a few months ago there was a mass shooting in Lewiston. The shooter had been in the military and likely would have met the qualifications to obtain a concealed weapon permit. We do not need a potential mass shooter to be bringing a weapon into our schools.
3) We have children in our schools with emotional and behavior health issues. An outsider with a concealed weapon has no way to know if these behaviors are dangerous. The risk to one of our students with special needs is too great.
4) Parental consent. Some parents simply don't want their children around guns. When children are at school, parents are trusting the school to be safe and gun free. Would parents have a say about the possibility that someone with a loaded weapon is in proximity to their child? I certainly do not want anyone who feels the need to carry a loaded concealed weapon everywhere they go, to be anywhere near my grandchildren.
5) There have been numerous accounts of guns being brought into schools by staff and accidentally left in the bathroom or some other location with student getting their hands on the weapon. It is just not safe for our children.
6) No one is allowed into the State House with a gun. Individuals are required to pass through a metal detector before entering. How are school staff supposed to feel safe with the knowledge that anyone entering the school could have a gun, or that the parents sitting across from them at a parent teacher conference could be armed? What if that parent did not like what the teacher was saying? This puts the teacher's life in danger. At sporting events a person could be sitting in the stands watching the game with a loaded gun on their person. These events can get heated. What assurance do we have that the person wearing the gun is not going to have a mental breakdown and start shooting?
7) Guns do not belong in schools under any circumstances. If someone enters the building with a gun that is cause for alarm and for a lockdown to be ordered. School staff simply do not know the mental state, motivation or qualifications of the individual with the gun. If concealed weapon holders are permitted to bring a handgun into a school how are staff supposed to know the difference between that individual and a potential school shooter?
I urge you to vote against this ridiculous bill.
Sincerely, Cathy Harris

Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy, and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee, I am Eileen King, the Deputy Executive Director for Maine School Management Association, testifying on behalf of the legislative committees of the Maine School Boards Association and the Maine School Superintendents Association in opposition to L.D. 885 and L.D. 525. Both proposed bills present significant risks to the safety of our students, school staff, and communities. Allowing firearms on or near school property in these ways would undermine the critical work that schools do to keep students safe and create an environment conducive to learning.
L.D. 885 proposes that individuals with a concealed carry permit be allowed to possess and discharge firearms on school property. While the intent behind this bill may be to provide security, the reality is that introducing more firearms into our schools does not make our students safer, as it opens the door to increased risk of violence or accidental discharge. Schools are places of learning and safety, and we must ensure that they remain free from the potential dangers of firearms.
L.D. 525 seeks to allow the discharge of firearms within 500 feet of school property in certain circumstances. This proposal significantly undermines the critical work schools do in creating safe, nurturing environments for students to learn. Even if the intent of this bill is tied to defending premises, the presence of gunfire in the vicinity of a school can cause serious harm and panic among students and staff. The sounds of gunshots can induce fear, disrupt the learning environment, and cause psychological trauma, particularly in the wake of national tragedies related to school shootings.
Allowing concealed weapons on school property would create confusion for staff and law enforcement, who would be unable to distinguish between those legally carrying firearms and those with malicious intent. This could lead to dangerous confrontations and heightened anxiety among both students and staff, impeding the positive, focused learning environment that schools strive to maintain.
The presence of firearms in schools has also been shown to increase the risk of violence rather than reduce it. In times of crisis, the presence of additional weapons can escalate a situation, making it more difficult for law enforcement to respond effectively. We must prioritize strategies that improve school safety through de-

escalation techniques and mental health support, not through the introduction of more weapons into these environments.
Both bills propose changes that could compromise the safety of our schools, the well-being of our students, and the effectiveness of the educators who work tirelessly to foster safe learning environments. We urge you to consider the potential consequences and to reject these bills. Our schools must remain sanctuaries for learning, free from the risks associated with firearms.
Resources: 1. Studies on Firearms and School Safety: Research shows that the introduction of firearms into schools increases the risk of accidents, violence, and intimidation. For example, a study by the National Education Association suggests that even the perception of weapons in school can contribute to a less secure environment, creating an atmosphere of fear. (National Education Association, The Impact of Guns on School Safety). 2. Psychological Impact of Gunfire Near Schools: Psychological research has demonstrated that exposure to gun violence, even indirectly through sound, can cause severe emotional and mental stress for students. This can result in increased anxiety, panic attacks, and post-traumatic stress disorder, which disrupts learning and creates lasting trauma. (American Psychological Association, Gun Violence and Its Effects on Children). 3. Law Enforcement Confusion: According to law enforcement experts, increased numbers of firearms in public spaces make it harder for officers to differentiate between law-abiding citizens and potential threats, raising the likelihood of dangerous confrontations during emergency responses. (FBI, Firearm Laws and Public Safety).

Testimony in OPPOSITION to: � LD 525, An Act to Strengthen Maine Citizens' Second Amendment Rights by Allowing the Discharge of Firearms on Private Property That Is Within 500 Feet of School Property in Certain Circumstances � LD 885, An Act to Allow Certain Persons with a Permit to Carry Concealed Handguns to Possess or Discharge a Firearm on School Property
Education and Cultural Affairs Committee May 7, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Esteemed Members of the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs,
My name is Madeleine DesFosses, and I am submitting this testimony on behalf of the Maine Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics. The Maine AAP is a professional organization of 300 pediatricians and pediatric subspecialists dedicated to protecting the health of Maine children and adolescents. We are in strong opposition to LD 525 and LD 885, which will make schools and students more susceptible to firearm related injuries and deaths.
The 500-foot buffer currently in place exists to protect students, teachers, and school communities from firearm-related violence. Eliminating this important buffer increases the risk of accidental discharges, misfires, stray bullets, and misunderstandings, all of which can have serious and potentially fatal consequences. We must ensure that schools remain safe spaces where students can learn and grow.
To that end, allowing concealed firearms onto school property unnecessarily puts the safety of students and staff at great risk. While the gun lobby falsely argues that "gun-free zones" only invite mass shootings, research shows that existing laws that prohibit weapons in schools help keep students safe. One study in Saint Louis, Missouri showed that there were nearly 14% fewer crimes committed with a firearm in gun-free school zones compared to gun-allowing zones (1).
Firearm related injuries are the leading cause of death among children and adolescents in the US. Therefore, we should be doing everything we can to prevent gun violence and protect our kids. That means prioritizing evidence-based policies that prevent and reduce firearm injuries, not policies like LD 525 and LD 885 perpetuate firearm violence and put children's lives at greater risk.
I urge the committee to vote "Ought NOT to Pass" on LD 525 and LD 885. Please help keep our schools and students safe.
Madeleine DesFosses Advocacy and Public Health Manager, Maine AAP

References: 1. Paul M. Reeping et al., "The Effect of Gun-free School Zones on Crimes Committed with a Firearm in Saint Louis, Missouri," Journal of Urban Health 100, no. 6 (2023): 1118-1127.

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and other distinguished members of the joint standing committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, my name is Lieutenant Mathew Casavant, and I am here to represent the Maine State Police and the Maine Department of Public Safety to testify in opposition of LD 885, "An Act to Allow Certain Persons with a Permit to Carry Concealed Handguns to Possess or Discharge a Firearm on School Property."
The Maine Department of Public Safety and Maine State Police is opposed to LD 885 due to possible safety concerns. As an officer, responding to a report of an active shooter or armed person at a school is one of the most stressful, chaotic, and emotional experiences that a police officer will ever encounter. Although highly trained, a police officer in this situation is likely to experience heightened levels of adrenaline and cortisol coursing through their body as it reacts to the stress they are facing. The officer may also experience "tunnel vison" and "auditory exclusion" as they enter the school in search of a shooter or armed subject and will rely on their training to stop the active threat. Information regarding the suspect(s) identity will likely be limited, meaning the police officer will have to react to what they are observing in real time. As a result, you can understand that if a police officer in this situation encounters a concerned citizen that is also armed with a handgun and not identified in anyway as a police officer, it could potentially result in a tragedy and, at minimum, slow the officer's response.
Another potential safety concern is the reality that a handgun that is concealed is not always truly hidden. Handguns come in different sizes, shapes, and colors and so do the holsters and packs that contain them. Additionally, some handguns are more suitable than others for concealed carry purposes. There are times when it becomes obvious that someone is carrying a handgun, namely when a handgun is carried under a tight shirt or becomes inadvertently exposed when bending over, such as to pick up a backpack or get a drink from a water fountain. Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association
In Opposition to
LD 885 - An Act to Allow Certain Persons with a Permit to Carry Concealed Handguns to Possess or Discharge a Firearm on School Property
May 7, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and members of the Education & Cultural Affairs Committee, my name is Rebecca Graham, and I am providing testimony in opposition to LD 885 on behalf of the Maine Municipal Association's (MMA) elected 70-member Legislative Policy Committee (LPC). MMA is a nonpartisan, nonprofit member service organization and aims to help provide policy solutions that work for all residents in Maine and the LPC guides the advocacy efforts and establishes positions on bills of municipal interest.
The only weapons that should be allowed in a school setting are those carried by well trained, annually certified, clearly identifiable school resource officers who are currently certified law enforcement officers. The role of a police officer in a school setting extends far beyond physical security. These professionals are deeply connected to their school community and establish important schoolcommunity relationships. These officers usually are armed, and in uniform, making them distinguishable in an emergency by outside responders should that be necessary.
The act of passing a 5 year limited look back on criminal history that enables an individual to obtain a concealed handgun permit does not mean that an individual is trained adequately to safely carry in a child centered facility. Not all risky behavior prohibits an individual from obtaining a concealed permit, and the permit process only allows for a 5 year review of possibly risky behavior that does not result in a charge to be considered in the discretionary elements of the review process.
A non-law enforcement officer carrying a weapon in a school is a liability to the safety of first responders, indistinguishable from an armed perpetrator, and unlikely to carry enough personal liability insurance to mitigate the risk for potential lawsuits occurring from negligent behavior if they are not employees of the school district. If they are employees of the school, this would force a municipality to assume greater liability for tort claims protections and result in an uncontrollable fiscal note as the act of carrying a concealed handgun permit alone is not proof of skill or lack of risk.
As noted in previous testimony, well trained individuals are encouraged to join any police department where they will learn more vital community skills necessary and needed by schools for safety and security. Officials ask that you protect first responders from needing to sort through potential threats in these spaces by only allowing certified law enforcement the authority to carry weapons in schools and vote ought not to pass on LD 885.
